description.p: An aarch64 build of Plex Media Player that runs the current Plex desktop web client. Playback uses mpv. Hardware decoding is used where the system provides it, through a stateful V4L2 decoder or VA-API. Decoding falls back to software for any stream the hardware cannot decode correctly, which on a device whose decoder emits only 8 bit frames includes 10 bit, HDR and Dolby Vision video.
The Plex web client is downloaded from Plex at install time as extra data and is covered by Plex's own terms.

ul.li: Changing a 3D setting while a file was playing stopped the app responding, and it would then not quit. The 3D settings are held in the same group as the video settings, and a change to any setting in that group re-applied the whole video configuration to the player, the decoder included, part way through a stream. Each video setting is now sent to the player only when its value has actually changed, so a 3D setting no longer touches playback at all.
The 3D section comes before the key list in the settings menu.
The key list is behind a button, so the settings list is shorter.

Started from the Steam icon with 3D through the headset turned on, the app showed a black screen and stopped before the Plex interface loaded. The headset check was made while the window was still being built, and the helper it starts on the host and the window itself were both asking the compositor for a surface at the same time. The check is now made when the settings menu is opened and when a 3D file starts playing, so it never coincides with the window being built.
3D through the headset is off by default again.
The log records when the headset check starts, which route it takes and how it ended.

The packing of a 3D file is now worked out when playback starts. The file's own 3D tag is used when it carries one, otherwise the file name is read for the usual markings, otherwise the shape of the picture is used. Half and full width are told apart by the display aspect, because the tag does not record which it is. The result is written to the log on every file.

A setting that says which packing to use, for files that carry no tag or are marked wrongly: left as worked out, side-by-side half or full width, over-under half or full height, or 2D. The settings menu shows what was worked out and where that came from.
A setting that swaps the left and right eye, for files packed the other way round.
Stereoscopic 3D is now on by default. Probing the runtime happens in the background and does not delay startup.

The settings button stays visible while a 3D file plays, so the packing can be changed without stopping playback. It moves to the middle of the right edge while it is showing over video, clear of the player's own controls.

A Stereoscopic 3D section in the settings menu, off by default. With it on, the app reports which OpenXR runtime answered, which headset it names and the resolution it recommends per eye, and a button draws to both eyes once to prove a session can be created. Stereoscopic playback is not implemented yet; this is the part it needs.

A separate program, pmp-xr-host, that does the headset work outside the sandbox. Flatpak always puts the app in its own process namespace and SteamVR's OpenXR runtime will not create a session inside one, so the runtime is reached through a program started on the host instead. The app reads its answer and nothing else changes.
The app may now talk to org.freedesktop.Flatpak, which is what starting that program requires.

A Steam section in the settings menu. It adds a Plex icon to your Steam library, writes that icon again if it was changed or deleted, and restarts Plex through Steam. Started from Steam, the device runs Plex on the performance profile it reserves for games, which is what 4K playback needs. Steam reads its shortcut list when it starts, so a new icon appears once Steam has restarted. The existing list is copied into the app's own data directory before anything is written to it.
On a headset, the app offers to add that icon the first time it is started outside Steam, and stops offering it if you answer never. The buttons in the settings menu remain either way.

The startup log now records whether Steam started the app, and on a device with SteamVR installed whether the OpenXR runtime answers, which headset it reports and the resolution it recommends per eye. Stereoscopic playback is not implemented; this is the groundwork for it.
Re-worked scenarios where the client would be logged out to prompt the user to log back in, either automatically or login from the cog where the user may be stuck at a constant loading screen.

The app sends the client to the Plex sign-in page by itself when the client reports ready and no Plex account session appears within twenty seconds. A device whose session has lapsed otherwise sits on the Home screen with a loading spinner and nothing to act on.

An Online Media Sources item in the settings menu, which opens the Plex page of that name. Its Discover Source setting removes the Trending and Activity tabs from Home, which report an error on this client. It is a Plex account setting and applies to every Plex app the account signs in to.
The Sign in to Plex item appears only when the client has no Plex account session.
Hardware video decoding through the system's stateful V4L2 decoder, for H.264, HEVC and VP9 where the device provides one. On the Steam Frame this takes 8 bit video off the CPU.

The hardware decoder is offered only for streams it can emit correctly. 10 bit, HDR and Dolby Vision video decodes in software, because a decoder that emits only 8 bit frames decodes 10 bit video into 8 bit samples without reporting an error.
The settings cog is hidden while video is on screen.
The Flatpak takes --device=all, which is what gives the sandbox the /dev/video* decoder nodes. Flatpak has no narrower option for them.
The settings menu and the update prompt take all keyboard, gamepad and mouse input while they are open, so the Plex interface behind them no longer responds.
An update is no longer offered when the installed build is newer than the published release. The comparison uses the build's time of day as well as its date.
The provider list sends the storage feature only in its JSON form.
A settings menu inside the app, opened with F1 or the gamepad's Menu button.

Update checks, with a manual check, a choice of cadence and release notes. The check compares the installed build's commit against the one the update repository publishes, so a rebuilt release is detected.
A download folder setting, with an option to confirm each download.
Text size and high contrast settings for the app's own screens.
Gamepad input, read through SDL.
Update reports arriving during an install no longer replace the install in progress.
A skipped version is recorded by the build's commit rather than by release tag.
Release notes are reached from the settings menu instead of a keyboard shortcut.
The settings list has a scroll bar and scrolls smoothly from the gamepad.
